title: Song of Songs
subtitle: the best song, a book of love without a name for God
lead: The Song of Songs is eight chapters of Hebrew love poetry. A woman and a man speak to each other and about each other, with a chorus of 'daughters of Jerusalem'. They praise one another's bodies in pictures of gazelles, towers, gardens and spices; they long for each other in the spring and at night; they search for each other in the city; and they say 'I belong to my lover and my lover belongs to me'. The title calls it the best of songs and ties it to Solomon.

Almost nothing in it says what it is for. It has no law, no history and no prayer. The LORD is not named, except possibly in the 'flame of Yah' of 8:6. Jews and Christians for most of two thousand years read it as the love of God for Israel, or of Christ for the Church or the soul, and the allegory shaped worship and prayer. Most scholars today read it first as poetry about human love. This scroll gives the Hebrew in plain English, explains the images, and sets the readings side by side.
facts: Not named. The title says 'of Solomon' (1:1), and tradition made Solomon the author. Many scholars think the poems are by several poets and were gathered later.
Debated: Solomon's time (about 950 BC), the northern kingdom before 722 BC, the Persian period (500s–300s BC), or the early Greek period (about 300–200 BC).
The land of Israel, from Lebanon and Hermon in the north to En-gedi in the south; vineyards, gardens and walled towns; a king's court and a mother's house.
Love poetry, with four descriptive praises of the body (wasf songs), dialogues, and a refrain. Read by most Jews and Christians before about 1800 as allegory.
Hebrew, with a few words from Persian (pardes) and possibly Greek (apiryon)
8 chapters, 117 verses (the Hebrew numbers 6:13 as 7:1, so Hebrew chapters 6 and 7 have 12 and 14 verses)

audience.to: The poems' first hearers are not named. The proposals include the guests at a wedding week, the pupils and scribes of a school, the court of a king, and the worshiping community of Judah after the exile, which kept the Song in its Writings. The people inside the poem are a woman, a man, the 'daughters of Jerusalem', her brothers and the city's watchmen.
audience.why: The book never says. As love poetry it praises the love between a man and a woman and teaches the young to hold it neither cheap nor sold: 'do not wake love until it wants to' (2:7; 3:5; 8:4), love 'cannot be bought' (8:7), and a woman's 'own vineyard' is hers (8:12). Read as the Jews and the Church read it, it teaches God's love for his people. Knowing the audience changes the reading: at a wedding the poems are songs of praise and blessing; in a school they are a model of the art of love poetry; in the Temple community they are a book of Scripture, kept for a reason beyond the poems' first use.
views: J. G. Wetzstein's account of Syrian village weddings in the 1800s, used by Franz Delitzsch, describes a week in which the couple are 'king and queen', the bride is praised limb by limb and dances the sword dance. Mishnah Taanit 4:8 tells how on the fifteenth of Av the daughters of Jerusalem danced in the vineyards in borrowed white clothes to be seen by young men. Both suggest a world in which songs like these were sung.
Michael Fox, who counts thirty-one poems in the Song, sees them as separate songs gathered by scribes. Some scholars place the collecting in the Persian or Hellenistic period, in a school of wisdom.

Those who hold the Song to be early see it as a product of the royal court of the tenth century BC, when Solomon's reign brought the imports and the court's culture that the Song's images reflect (1 Kings 4:32; 10).

The Jewish people kept the Song as holy because they read it as God's love song for Israel. The rabbis (Akiva, Mishnah Yadayim 3:5) and the Targum make this the book's purpose. Monks and nuns later took it as their rule of prayer.

authorship: The title says 'of Solomon' (1:1), and 1 Kings 4:32 says he wrote 1,005 songs. Jewish and Christian tradition held him to be the author. Defenders point to the book's royal setting, its imported spices (1 Kings 10) and its animal and plant names. Duane Garrett argues for Solomon as author or patron.

Tirzah, the capital of the northern kingdom, is set beside Jerusalem (6:4). The book has northern-sounding words, such as the she- relative instead of asher. Some scholars place the poems in the northern kingdom in the 800s or 700s BC.

The Persian word pardes (4:13), the she- relative, Aramaic-like forms, and the Song's likeness to the late books of the Writings suggest a date after the exile. Roland Murphy allows the Persian or early Greek period.

The word apiryon (3:9) may be Greek, and the Song's likeness to Theocritus's pastoral poems and to Greek love poetry has been cited. Michael Fox allows the late Persian or early Hellenistic period but notes how little the language can prove.

Many scholars say the language allows too many dates and that poems of this kind could come from any period in which Hebrew was written (Exum, Longman). The book's place in the canon does not depend on a date.
outline: First cycle: her longing, the daughters of Jerusalem, 'dark and lovely', where he pastures, praise in the green bed, the banquet house; the oath (2:7)
Spring and the night search: 'Listen! My lover!', 'Get up, my darling', the little foxes, the search in the city; the oath (3:5)
The wedding: Solomon's litter, the first praise of the bride (4:1–7), 'my sister, my bride', the locked garden, the garden opened (5:1)
The knock and the second night search, the watchmen, the praise of the lover (5:10–16), 'my lover has gone down to his garden'
His praise again, the Shulammite, the dance of the two camps, the praise from the feet up
'His desire is toward me', 'let us go out to the fields', 'if only you were my brother'; the oath (8:4)
The seal and the flame, the little sister and the wall, Solomon's vineyard and hers, 'Hurry, my lover'

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: The title and Solomon, the date and language (the she- relative, the Persian pardes, the Greek or Persian apiryon, Tirzah beside Jerusalem), the places from Lebanon to En-gedi, and why a book without God's name was kept.

lenses.name: Love poetry
lenses.desc: The Song read as human love: a collection or one poem, its voices and its praise-songs, and its neighbors in Egyptian love songs, Sumerian songs of Dumuzi and Inanna, Syrian wedding songs and Greek pastoral. Fox, Exum, Murphy, Longman, Garrett, Bloch, Keel.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: Akiva's 'holy of holies' (Mishnah Yadayim 3:5), the Targum's history of Israel from the Exodus to the Messiah, Song of Songs Rabbah, Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Maimonides, the Kabbalists, and the reading at Passover and on Friday evenings.

lenses.name: Christian tradition
lenses.desc: Allegory of Christ and the Church or the soul (Hippolytus, Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, Ambrose, Augustine, Bernard, Teresa of Ávila, John of the Cross), the Marian liturgy, the Reformation (Luther, Calvin, Castellio, the Puritans), and the modern marriage reading, including the 'theology of the body'.

lenses.name: Modern and women's readings
lenses.desc: The woman's voice and initiative (Trible's 'Eden reversed', Exum, Brenner, Falk, Bloch), what the brothers and the watchmen show about her freedom, readings in dialogue with desire, consent and marriage today, and the drama theories (Ewald's shepherd-lover and Delitzsch's two-character drama, which argued against the shepherd).

sections.b:
The Plain English text is made from the Masoretic Text (the Leningrad Codex, with the Aleppo Codex where the word list marks it) and follows it throughout; the verses where it parts company with the Greek or the Dead Sea Scrolls are in the variants. It is poetry, one verse to a line, with ' / ' between the lines of a verse.

Verse numbers are English. The Hebrew Bible numbers 6:13 as 7:1, so its chapter 7 begins one verse earlier than ours (see the note at 6:13).

The Hebrew marks the speaker by gender and number, but the text has no labels, and the Plain adds none inside the verses. The headings name each unit and the settings cards give the likely voices. Where the speaker or the break is debated (1:8; 1:9–11; 2:15; 4:16–5:1; 6:10; 7:10; 8:5; 8:8–9; 8:11–12) the notes give each view.

A few words are kept the same everywhere: dod is 'my lover' and dodim 'lovemaking'; ra'yah is 'my darling'; ahavah is always 'love'; each spice is one English word; and body words (breasts, belly, thighs, navel) are given plainly, with the sense explained in a note and no euphemism added or removed. The term list lives in the site's shared list.

Shir hashirim is a superlative, like 'holy of holies': the best of songs. The little word le- in lishlomo can mean 'by', 'for', 'about', 'in the manner of' or 'belonging to the collection of'. Solomon is named seven times (1:1, 5; 3:7, 9, 11; 8:11, 12). First Kings 4:32 says he wrote 1,005 songs, and Sirach 47:14–17 praises his songs and riddles. In 8:12 the woman sets 'my own vineyard' beside his thousand, so the king may be the lover, a stock figure of royal luxury, or a foil to a lover who is a shepherd.

Two views divide scholars. Michael Fox, followed by Roland Murphy in part, treats the Song as an anthology of separate poems (Fox counts thirty-one), joined by repeated lines, a shared stock of images, and the editor's hand. Others, such as J. Cheryl Exum, Tremper Longman and Duane Garrett, find one poem with a refrain structure, in which the oath at 2:7, 3:5 and 8:4 and the refrain 'my lover belongs to me and I belong to him' at 2:16, 6:3 and 7:10 mark its stages. The repeated lines in 4:1–3 and 6:5–7, the three questions 'Who is this?' (3:6; 6:10; 8:5), and the return to the gazelle at the end (2:9, 17; 8:14) are cited on both sides.

sections.h: Four ways of reading the Song
sections.b:
Allegory. The lover is God and the woman Israel (the Targum, Song of Songs Rabbah, Rashi), or Christ and the Church or the soul (Hippolytus, Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, Ambrose, Bernard). This was by far the most common reading from the rabbis and the Fathers until the 1700s and still carries weight in Jewish and Catholic teaching.

Love poetry. A celebration of human love, with no hidden meaning. This is the reading of most scholars since the 1800s, and the Song's closest parallels (Egyptian love songs, Syrian wedding songs) support it. Some add that the Song describes marriage as a gift of God.

Drama. A story with two characters (Solomon and the Shulammite) or three (a shepherd lover as well, to whom the Shulammite stays true against Solomon). Origen already called the Song a wedding poem in dramatic form. Ewald and, after him, Ginsburg developed the three-character version with a shepherd lover; Delitzsch held the two-character form (Solomon and the Shulammite) and argued against the shepherd reading. Few scholars hold either now, because the text has no stage directions.

Wedding or cultic liturgy. The poems were sung at weddings or at a festival of sacred marriage (Wetzstein; Pope on Mesopotamian songs). Combinations are common: love poetry with a typological echo, or an anthology of love songs read as allegory once it was in the canon.

Consensus: most modern scholars read the Song first as love poetry; most Jews and Christians before about 1800 read it as allegory.

The Song's Hebrew mixes old and late forms. For a late date: the she- relative (instead of asher) used throughout, the Persian loanword pardes (4:13), possibly the Greek word apiryon (3:9, litter), and some Aramaic-like forms. For an early or northern date: Tirzah as a city of beauty beside Jerusalem (6:4), which stopped being the northern capital after about 880 BC; the northern place names; and the likeness to Egyptian love songs of the 1300s–1100s BC. Defenders of an early date answer that the she- relative was a northern or dialect form and that Persian and Greek loanwords could have reached Israel early, through trade. No view has won.

sections.h: Why a book without God's name was kept
sections.b:
The Mishnah records Rabbi Akiva's saying that the Song is the holy of holies (Mishnah Yadayim 3:5) and a dispute over whether it 'defiles the hands', the rabbis' term for a holy book. Tosefta Sanhedrin 12:10 condemns anyone who sings it in a banquet house, as if it were a mere song. Avot de-Rabbi Natan (version A, chapter 1) lists it among the books once considered for withdrawal. The Song is one of the five Scrolls read in the synagogue (at Passover). Origen (about AD 240) reports a Jewish rule that none should read it before maturity. Jerome (Letter 107, to Laeta) advises delay until a girl is grown.

In the Christian church the Song's place was not seriously questioned. Theodore of Mopsuestia (about AD 400) is reported by later writers to have rejected the allegorical reading, and the Council of Constantinople in 553 is often said to have condemned him for it. The surviving acts concern his Christology, and whether the Song was part of the charge is disputed. In 1544 Sebastian Castellio, seeking ordination in Geneva, called the Song a lascivious love poem, and the ministers, under Calvin, refused him.

The LORD is not named in the Song. The only possible divine name is the ending -yah of shalhevetyah in 8:6, and it may only intensify the word ('a raging flame'). The book has no covenant, law, temple, sin or prayer. Each reading deals with this silence differently. The allegories say that God is the hidden speaker; the love-poetry reading says that the book honors a gift of the creation without turning it into something else, a position near the wisdom books; the wisdom reading says that enjoying love is among the things God gives (Ecclesiastes 9:9). The note at 8:6 gives the views.

The Targum of the Song (a long Aramaic paraphrase, probably from the 600s–700s AD) retells the Song as the history of Israel, from the Exodus to the coming of the Messiah, with God as the lover. Song of Songs Rabbah (about AD 600) and Rashi (died 1105) read it the same way, and Maimonides used it to describe the love of God. Jewish custom reads it at Passover and sings 'Lekha Dodi', based on it, on Friday evenings. Among Christians, Hippolytus (about AD 200) wrote the first commentary; Origen (about AD 240) set the pattern of the soul's ascent; Gregory of Nyssa (about 390s) and Ambrose followed. Bernard of Clairvaux preached 86 sermons on the Song (1135–1153) and reached only 3:1. The Latin liturgy turned verses of the Song into Marian texts. John of the Cross wrote the Spiritual Canticle (1578–1586) and Teresa of Ávila her Meditations from it. Luther read it as Solomon's praise of good government, and the Puritans as Christ's love for the believer. Today Christians also read it as a celebration of married love, and John Paul II's 'theology of the body' draws on it.

sections.h: The witnesses and what was checked
sections.b:
The base text is the Leningrad Codex, with the Aleppo Codex and the Ketiv and Qere marks (1:17; 2:11, 13; 4:9; 6:12 and the small spellings at 3:8; 6:3; 7:8; 8:1, 13). The Septuagint was read in Swete's printing of Codex Vaticanus. It is very literal in this book, and in a few places reads the vowels differently (1:2, 4; 4:10 'breasts'; 4:12 'garden'; 5:1 'brothers'; 6:12 'Aminadab'; 7:9 'lips and teeth'; 7:10 'turning'; 8:6 with no divine name) or the words differently (2:7, 3:5 and 8:4, where the animals of the oath become 'the powers and the forces of the field').

The Dead Sea Scrolls were read in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription. 6Q6 preserves parts of 1:1–7. 4QCant-b (4Q107) preserves 2:9–3:2, 3:5, 3:9–11, 4:1–3, 4:8–11 and 4:14–5:1. 4QCant-a (4Q106) preserves 3:4–5, 3:7–4:7 and 6:11–7:6, and 4QCant-c (4Q108) 3:7–8. Both larger scrolls are shorter than the Masoretic text in this transcription, but in different places: 4QCant-b goes from 3:5 to 3:9 (no 3:6–8) and from 4:3 to 4:8 (no 4:4–7), and 4QCant-a goes from 4:7 to 6:11 (no 4:8–6:10). 4QCant-a also has only one pair of 'come back' in 6:13, and 4QCant-b lacks 'or a young deer' at 2:17. Emanuel Tov, who edited the scrolls (DJD XVI), is the standard reference for these shorter readings. The fragments are small, and they cannot show that the Song was normally shorter at Qumran. The variants list these places.

The Targum is cited from Philip Alexander's translation (The Aramaic Bible 17A) and the Latin Vulgate from the Weber–Gryson edition.

About fifty Egyptian love songs survive from the New Kingdom, in Papyrus Chester Beatty I, the Turin papyrus, Papyrus Harris 500 and the Cairo Love Songs; Michael Fox compared them to the Song in detail (1985). They share the Song's 'sister' and 'brother' for lovers, the sickness of love, gardens, and birds. The Sumerian songs of Dumuzi and Inanna have apples, milk, a door opened to a lover. Greek pastoral poetry (Theocritus, about 270 BC) is a later parallel. J. G. Wetzstein's account of Syrian wedding week (1873) offers a model of the wasf and the sword dance. These show the Song belongs to a family; they do not show where it came from.

spec.title: The three 'Who is this?' questions as a staircase
spec.body: The question 'Who is this coming up?' comes three times: 3:6 (from the wilderness, in smoke, in a king's litter), 6:10 (looking down like the dawn, moon and sun) and 8:5 (climbing up, leaning on her lover). I suggest they trace the woman's rise from a distant, perfumed procession, to a figure who towers over the sky, to a woman who has come home and leans on her man. Commentators often note the repeated question; the reading of the three as a staircase of rising nearness is my own, and it may overlap with published structural studies that use the questions as markers.
spec.refs: Song of Songs 3:6; Song of Songs 6:10; Song of Songs 8:5

spec.title: Two vineyards frame the book
spec.body: The woman's complaint in 1:6 (her brothers made her guard the vineyards but her own she did not guard) and her answer in 8:11–12 (Solomon has his vineyard to rent, but 'my own vineyard is in front of me') bracket the book. I suggest the whole Song is the story of how she comes to keep her own vineyard, with the oaths, the night searches and the dance as stages. Exum and Trible both note the vineyard motif and the woman's growing freedom; the framing of the whole book by these two verses is my own proposal.
spec.refs: Song of Songs 1:6; Song of Songs 2:15; Song of Songs 8:11–12

prompts:
A young woman in a plain dyed robe stands inside a stone house, one hand on a wooden lattice; outside, on a hillside of spring flowers, a lean young man leaps down over rocks like a gazelle. Wild crocuses, blossoming fig and vine, a turtledove on a ledge.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment scroll. Sepia and iron-gall ink linework with charcoal shading, red-ochre and yellow-ochre pigment like cave paintings, simple register lines like an ancient Near Eastern frieze, and a few bold flat shapes of deep blue in the manner of modern paper cut-outs. Visible parchment grain, uneven hand-drawn lines, soft torn irregular edges that fade into the parchment. No frame, no rectangular border, no sharp-edged square image, no text.

A procession coming up out of a dry hill country at dawn: a carrying litter with silver posts and a purple seat, a ring of sixty armed men with swords on their thighs, a column of fragrant smoke rising behind, a small group of women in white watching from a hill. Cedar branches from Lebanon in the foreground.

A walled garden seen from above through an open gate: pomegranate trees, nard and henna bushes, a spring in the center, a tall cedar of Lebanon beyond the wall, two winds drawn as swirls of line from the north and south. The gate is open. A pair of hands, one man's and one woman's, hold the key.

A woman and man side by side on a hillside, she with her hand on a carved stone seal on a cord at his chest; behind them a tall flame rises from an altar-like rock, and wide flood waters break against it and do not reach it. Two vineyards in the distance, one with a small stone tower and workers, one a single plot with a woman guarding it.

reading: Michael V. Fox, The Song of Songs and the Ancient Egyptian Love Songs (1985)
The standard comparison with the Egyptian songs; argues for an anthology of thirty-one poems.
J. Cheryl Exum, Song of Songs (Old Testament Library, 2005)
A careful literary and feminist commentary, arguing for one poem and a woman's voice.
Roland E. Murphy, The Song of Songs (Hermeneia, 1990)
A full historical commentary with a history of interpretation.
Tremper Longman III, Song of Songs (NICOT, 2001)
An evangelical commentary that reads the book as one poem of human love with a place in wisdom.
Duane Garrett, Song of Songs (Word Biblical Commentary 23B, 2004)
A conservative commentary arguing for Solomonic origin and for a unified poem.
Ariel and Chana Bloch, The Song of Songs (1995)
A poets' translation with a notable introduction and notes.
Phyllis Trible, God and the Rhetoric of Sexuality (1978), the chapter on the Song of Songs
The influential reading of the Song as Eden restored.
Marvin H. Pope, Song of Songs (Anchor Bible, 1977)
The great storehouse of ancient parallels, with strong opinions.
Othmar Keel, The Song of Songs (Continental Commentary, 1994)
Reads the images with the help of ancient Near Eastern art.
Philip S. Alexander, The Targum of Canticles (Aramaic Bible 17A, 2003)
The Aramaic paraphrase in English, with notes.

traditions.q: What is the Song of Songs about?
views: The Church's tradition reads the Song as the love of Christ for the Church and for the soul, and also as the love of husband and wife, and does not choose between them. The spiritual senses rest on the literal (Catechism 115–119). Pope John Paul II's 'theology of the body' reads it as a poem of the gift of self in marriage that images Christ and the Church. Monks and nuns used it as their prayer (Bernard, Teresa of Ávila, John of the Cross).

The Fathers (Gregory of Nyssa and others) read the Song as the soul's ascent to God and the Church's love for Christ. The bridal-chamber language of the Bridegroom services of Holy Week rests on the parable of Matthew 25 and on the services' own hymns more than on the Song; the Song's main place is in monastic and mystical reading. The Church also honors marriage in its crowning service.

Luther's lectures (1530–31) read the Song as Solomon's praise of the good government God gave him, with the bride as his people; later Lutheran teachers read it as Christ and the Church, and modern Lutherans also as married love.

Calvin wrote no commentary on the Song, and in 1544 the Geneva ministers refused Sebastian Castellio ordination partly over his reading of it as a love poem. The Puritans, such as Richard Sibbes, loved the allegory of Christ and the believer; modern Reformed teachers such as Tremper Longman read it as poetry of married love.

Early Baptists such as John Gill read the Song as Christ's love for his church; many Baptist teachers today teach it as a celebration of marriage, often with a typological echo of Christ and the church.
Most evangelical teachers and commentators now read the Song as God's gift of married love, to be enjoyed within marriage, with some seeing a secondary picture of Christ and his people.
